public_rationale: The evidence supports a directional link between expanding AI computation and rising total electricity consumption [e1, e2]. In its June 2026 disclosure, Google reports an electricity-demand surge in 2025 and connects growing AI demand with increased energy requirements [e1]. Berkeley Lab reports that U.S. data-center power demand more than doubled between 2017 and 2023, largely because of AI server growth [e2]. Google researchers describe ways to improve serving efficiency, but the cited passage does not show that total electricity consumption fell [e3].
limitations: Google does not quantify AI's share of its electricity increase or give a percentage increase in the cited passage [e1].
Berkeley Lab covers U.S. data centers generally, without isolating individual big technology companies [e2].
The cited efficiency passage provides no measured reduction or comparison period [e3].
The evidence does not establish a fixed growth ratio, separate training from deployment growth, or establish the relationship for every company [e1, e2, e3].
The contract excludes the hedged statement that scaling is the only potent method from the scored claim.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: The only potent trick anyone seems to have is scaling, and the more scaling big tech companies do, the more power they will consume.
conditions: seems (applies to scaling being the only potent trick)

statement.excerpt: The only potent trick anyone seems to have is scaling, and the more scaling the big tech companies do, the more power they will consume.
statement.document_title: Eric Schmidt’s Risky Bet on AI and Climate Change

from_speaker: The only potent trick anyone seems to have is scaling
the more scaling the big tech companies do, the more power they will consume
if we continue on the current path
our_interpretation: The exclusivity statement is qualified by 'seems'. It is not scored as a definite assertion that no other effective method exists.
The firm, testable commitment is the directional link between expanding AI computation and increasing electricity consumption at big technology companies.

The ordinary reading concerns total electricity needed for larger training and deployment workloads along the described development path. It does not specify proportional growth, a minimum increase, or increasing electricity per individual query.
This is assessed as a causal relationship, not a forecast with an invented deadline. Later observations can test that relationship.
Efficiency improvements must be considered when assessing total consumption; constant efficiency is not assumed.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence links increased AI computation at big technology companies to rising total electricity consumption, with measurements or documented analysis supporting the causal explanation rather than merely showing unrelated company growth.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable evidence shows that expanding AI computation along the described path does not increase total electricity consumption, or establishes that the apparent electricity increase comes from other activities while AI electricity use remains flat or falls. Improvements per query alone do not establish this.

evidence.locator: Section 'Progressing toward our climate and energy moonshots requires significant innovation', second paragraph
evidence.explanation: Google reports a 37% annual electricity-demand increase and describes expanding AI demand and infrastructure as placing additional demands on energy systems. This supports the directional relationship, although the company does not separate AI electricity consumption from other workloads.

evidence.locator: Section 'Among the report’s key findings', third finding
evidence.explanation: The laboratory attributes much of the estimated historical increase to AI servers, providing independent support for the proposed mechanism. Its population is U.S. data centers generally, so it is contextual rather than a company-specific outcome measurement.

evidence.excerpt: a larger batch size prioritizes throughput and efficiency
evidence.locator: Section 2, discussion of production inference efficiency, item 1
evidence.explanation: The paper reports a 33-fold reduction in energy per median Gemini Apps text prompt between May 2024 and May 2025 and describes efficiencies enabled by production serving. This materially qualifies any fixed relationship between workload and electricity, but does not establish falling total consumption.
